title: Plan, organise and support project meetings and workshops

lessons.title: Planning a meeting or workshop
lessons.html:
Why plan?

In agri business, projects often bring many people together: a co-op launching a new grain intake system, a farmers' day with a seed company, a study group meeting, or a workshop to train silo staff on a new grading procedure. A meeting that is poorly planned wastes everyone's time and money, especially when farmers have driven long distances in harvest season. As a project support person, your job is to make sure the meeting achieves its purpose smoothly.

Start with the purpose

Ask the project leader: What must this meeting achieve? Is it to inform, to decide, to plan, or to train? The purpose decides who must attend, how long it should be and what format suits it. A decision meeting needs the people with authority; a training workshop needs the people who will do the work.

Planning checklist

ItemQuestions to answer
Date and timeAvoid planting, harvest and auction days. Allow travel time from outlying farms.
VenueSize, access, parking for bakkies and trailers, power, toilets, shade, mobile signal
ParticipantsWho must attend, who is optional, who needs to be informed
AgendaTopics, presenters, time per item, breaks
ResourcesProjector, screen, flipcharts, extension cords, generator if load-shedding is likely, handouts
CateringNumbers, dietary needs, water
BudgetVenue hire, catering, travel, materials; approval needed

The agenda

A good agenda lists the meeting's purpose, date, time, venue and each item with the person responsible and the time allowed. Send it with any reading material at least several working days before the meeting so participants can prepare. Put decision items early, while people are fresh.

Invitations and confirmations

Send invitations by the channel participants actually use; many farmers respond better to a WhatsApp message or a phone call than to email. Ask for RSVPs by a date and keep a list of confirmations. Send a reminder a day or two before.

lessons.title: Supporting the meeting on the day
lessons.html:
Before people arrive

  • Arrive early. Check the room set-up, seating, signage and the route from the gate.
  • Test the projector, laptop, microphone and internet. Have the presentation on a flash drive as a backup.
  • Prepare the attendance register. For accredited training workshops, the register is evidence and must be complete and signed.
  • Know where the emergency exits, first aid kit and fire extinguisher are, and who the first aider is.

During the meeting

The chairperson leads the meeting, but you support them:

  • Welcome participants and direct them to sign the register.
  • Keep time and give the chair discreet signals when an item runs over.
  • Distribute handouts at the right moment.
  • Solve problems quietly: a failed projector, too few chairs, a late caterer.
  • Take minutes, or support the minute-taker.

Taking minutes

Minutes are the official record. They do not need every word said, but must capture:

  1. Date, venue, attendees and apologies.
  2. Each agenda item, with a short summary of the discussion.
  3. Decisions taken, worded clearly.
  4. Actions: what, who and by when.

Example action: "Silo manager to obtain three quotes for a new moisture meter by 15 August."

Workshops

Workshops are more interactive than meetings. Plan group work, prepare flipcharts and markers, and arrange the room in groups rather than rows. Make sure language and level suit the participants; for farm workers you may need an interpreter.

Handling difficulties

If discussion becomes heated, support the chair in keeping to the agenda and to respectful behaviour. Note disagreements objectively in the minutes without taking sides.

lessons.title: After the meeting
lessons.html:
Following up

Much of the value of a meeting is lost if nothing happens afterwards. Your follow-up work turns decisions into action.

  1. Draft the minutes within a day or two while memory is fresh. Send them to the chair to check.
  2. Distribute approved minutes to all attendees and to those who sent apologies.
  3. Track actions. Keep an action list with owner and due date. Send reminders before due dates and report progress to the project leader.
  4. Settle costs. Collect invoices for venue, catering and travel, check them against what was ordered, and submit them for payment with the correct approvals.
  5. Return equipment and leave the venue clean.
  6. File records: agenda, attendance register, minutes, presentations, invoices. Workshop registers and evaluation forms may be needed for training records and Skills Development levy reporting.

Evaluating the meeting

Ask: Did we achieve the purpose? Did it start and end on time? Was the venue suitable? What went wrong and how can we prevent it next time? For workshops, a short evaluation form helps improve future sessions. Share lessons learned with the project team.

Protecting information

Attendance registers and contact lists contain personal information. Keep them secure and use them only for the purpose they were collected for, in line with POPIA.

Key points

  • Start with the purpose; it drives who attends and how the meeting runs.
  • Avoid peak farming dates and plan for power and connectivity problems.
  • Send the agenda and papers early and confirm attendance.
  • Minutes must record decisions and actions with owner and due date.
  • Follow up actions, settle costs and file records.
